item.title: The Coming ‘Nature Rights’ Tar-Pit Bureaucratic Nightmare
item.description: The “nature rights” movement would grant personhood and the “rights to exist, persist, maintain and regenerate its vital cycles, structure, functions and its processes in evolution” to geological features, ecological systems, flora and fauna, and indeed all that is. Enforcement would be a nightmare....
item.content:encoded:
The “nature rights” movement would grant personhood and the “rights to exist, persist, maintain and regenerate its vital cycles, structure, functions and its processes in evolution” to geological features, ecological systems, flora and fauna, and indeed all that is.

Enforcement would be a nightmare. Most grant universal court standing — meaning that anyone who believes that nature’s rights are being violated can sue. Other proposals appoint commissions to determine whether proposed or past human endeavors violate nature’s rights.

item.content:encoded:
The evidence that Chinese doctors harvest organs from murdered political prisoners, such as , is overwhelming. But evidence also shows that the means of death in some cases has been the organ procurement itself.

A new study reports that doctors who were demonstrated in a 2023 report (which I discussed here) to have so killed people have not only faced zero legal or professional consequences but have thrived in their medical careers. item.title: Euthanasia as Organ Farming

item.content:encoded:
When euthanasia is conjoined with organ donation, suicidal patients become objectified and may be treated differently than they would otherwise in order to maximize the efficacy of their organs — reducing them, in effect, to so many natural resources.

A new study makes that point clear. The report states that the first 100 organ harvesting after euthanasia in the Netherlands resulted in 408 transplanted organs.

Many will cheer. I won’t. As I have discussed repeatedly, donation conjoining can become the trigger that sparks the decision to be killed — or at least, its timing. For example, a 17-year-old Belgian brain cancer patient was put into a 36-hour coma before her euthanasia — not to prevent unbearable suffering but to test her organs and find suitable recipients. And she chose the “when” of her euthanasia to maximize their viability.

The report validates my criticism:

Healthcare professionals reported acute practical tensions between adherence to standard clinical protocols and the maintenance of patient comfort at the close of life. Specific points of friction included the enforcement of pre-procedural fasting requirements and the progressive medicalisation of the dying process through invasive physiological monitoring, both of which can compromise the dignity of the end-of-life environment.
Ethical complexities were particularly pronounced in cases involving donors with psychiatric conditions and early dementia. Clinical teams experienced substantial emotional and logistical demands while navigating these cases, though staff members consistently reported finding motivation in the meaningful clinical impact achieved for organ recipients and the fulfillment of donor wishes.

At that point, the organs have become more important than the patient. And note, there is no discussion of suicide prevention, because few if any patients who ask for euthanasia or assisted suicide ever receive such interventions that could save their lives.

Most killed donors were either mentally ill (31 percent) or had neurodegenerative disorders (52 percent) because of the quality of their organs, meaning that most were not terminally ill, at least in the sense of dying soon.

Killing and harvesting procedures are accomplished by euthanizing the patient in an ICU and then wheeling the body immediately into a surgical suite for procurement. The report’s conclusion:

This article highlights that the combined procedures require a delicate balance between maximising organ viability and protecting the patient’s experience of a dignified, non-medicalised death.

I agree being killed is not the practice of medicine — although the authors clearly don’t see it that way. But being killed in an ICU with all the accoutrements sure is medicalized.

Much is made in the study of how donating after euthanasia fulfills the suicidal person’s altruistic desires. If that is what counts — more than life itself — why have any limitations on suicidal persons being killed and donating for any reason? Think of the organs we could obtain for the use of people who still want to live!

And since suicide is becoming a fundamental human right — regardless of the reason — and is now the law in Germany and Estonia, why not? We are fast crafting a world out of the dark conjuring of Jack Kevorkian. Organ harvesting suicidal people was one of Dr. Death’s fever dreams, after all.

Where is all of this heading? Euthanasia by organ donation — already under serious discussion in bioethics and medical journals. When that happens, our transformation into pure utilitarianism in which human life only has relative value will become unstoppable. Lord have mercy.

item.title: New Organ Transplant Rule Allows Organ Procurement Surgeons to Cause Brain Death
item.description: The dead donor rule is the foundation of ethical organ transplant medicine. item.content:encoded:
The is the foundation of ethical organ transplant medicine. Under the DDR, vital organs can only be obtained from the bodies of deceased patients, and no patient can be killed to allow organ procurement.

The DDR is under great threat from bioethicists who want to end it — and from actual practice that has seen some transplant teams cross ethical boundaries. Thus, the recently decertified two organ-procurement organizations for egregious and repeated violations.
